papers.title: Mitochondrial quality-control states in cadmium neurotoxicity: Adaptive clearance, disproportionate elimination and stalled flux.
papers.summary: This paper examines how mitochondrial quality-control pathways, including mitophagy, respond to cadmium exposure in neurons. It identifies distinct mitochondrial states ranging from adaptive clearance of damaged mitochondria to excessive elimination and situations where mitophagy flux becomes stalled or blocked. These findings help characterize how heavy metal toxicity disrupts normal mitochondrial turnover and quality control mechanisms in the brain.
papers.why: Understanding how cadmium disrupts mitophagy flux and mitochondrial quality control in neurons directly informs the PhD project's focus on mitophagy dysregulation as a mechanism of neuronal stress or dysfunction.

papers.title: Unraveling the pyroptosis-mitophagy axis: from molecular mechanisms to therapeutic opportunities.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how two cellular processes—pyroptosis (a form of inflammatory cell death) and mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria)—interact with each other. It likely discusses the molecular signaling pathways that connect mitochondrial quality control to inflammatory cell death decisions. The review probably also highlights how targeting this axis could offer new therapeutic strategies for diseases involving excessive inflammation or cell death.
papers.why: Since mitophagy dysfunction is often linked to neuroinflammation and neuronal death, understanding the pyroptosis-mitophagy axis could provide mechanistic insight relevant to neurodegeneration and interneuron vulnerability in the brain.

papers.title: MiR-204-5p signalling modulates apoptosis and mitophagy-related changes after intracerebral hemorrhage in adult rats
papers.summary: This study investigates how miR-204-5p, a small regulatory RNA molecule, influences brain cell death and mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy) following intracerebral hemorrhage in adult rats. The researchers likely show that manipulating this microRNA affects the balance between apoptosis (programmed cell death) and mitophagy-related processes after brain bleeding injury. Findings suggest miR-204-5p could be a signaling node that determines whether damaged neurons survive or die after hemorrhagic stroke.
papers.why: This paper connects microRNA regulation to mitophagy in neurons after brain injury, offering molecular mechanisms relevant to the project's focus on neuronal mitophagy and autophagy pathways.

papers.title: The Glymphatic-Meningeal Lymphatic System and Autophagy in ME/CFS and Long COVID: A Mechanistic Perspective.
papers.summary: This paper proposes a mechanistic link between the brain's glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic drainage systems and cellular autophagy processes in the context of ME/CFS and Long COVID. It argues that impaired waste clearance via these pathways could contribute to neuroinflammation and fatigue symptoms seen in these conditions. The piece is a conceptual/review perspective rather than original experimental data.
papers.why: Although focused on a different disease context, this paper's discussion of autophagy dysregulation and impaired brain waste clearance offers conceptual background relevant to understanding neuronal autophagy and mitophagy disruption that could inform the broader framework of your mitophagy/autophagy research in brain tissue.

papers.title: Niosomal Mexiletine Attenuates Rotenone-Induced Parkinsonism via Modulation of the circDLGAP4/miR-134-5p/p-CREB Axis and Restoration of Mitochondrial-Autophagic Homeostasis.
papers.summary: This study tests a nano-formulated version of mexiletine (encapsulated in niosomes) as a treatment in a rotenone-induced rat model of Parkinson's disease. The treatment appears to work by altering a molecular pathway involving a circular RNA (circDLGAP4), a microRNA (miR-134-5p), and a signaling protein (p-CREB), which together influence mitochondrial function and autophagy. The researchers report that this treatment helps restore normal mitochondrial-autophagic balance and reduces Parkinsonian symptoms in the model.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it explores mitophagy and autophagy regulation in neurons via a specific molecular axis in a neurodegeneration model, which could inform mechanistic understanding or methodology relevant to the PhD project's core focus, even though it doesn't directly address spatial transcriptomics, interneurons, or perineuronal nets.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitochondrial morphology/autophagosome markers (e.g., LC3, Parkin, PINK1) alongside circDLGAP4/miR-134-5p/p-CREB expression levels across treatment groups would be most informative for assessing the mechanistic claims.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Transplantation as a Therapeutic Strategy: From Energy Replacement to Metabolic and Immune Reprogramming.
papers.summary: This paper reviews mitochondrial transplantation, a technique where healthy mitochondria are transferred into damaged or dysfunctional cells. It explores how this approach can restore cellular energy production but also reprogram metabolic and immune pathways in recipient cells. The review likely discusses therapeutic applications across various diseases where mitochondrial dysfunction plays a central role.
papers.why: Since mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control are central to this PhD project on neuronal health, understanding mitochondrial transplantation as a complementary or contrasting therapeutic strategy could inform interpretations of mitochondrial dynamics in interneurons and their surrounding microenvironment.

papers.title: Role and mechanism of action of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in nonylphenol-induced podocyte apoptosis and glomerulonephritis.
papers.summary: This study investigates how nonylphenol, an environmental pollutant, triggers kidney podocyte damage and apoptosis. It focuses on the PINK1/Parkin pathway, a key mitochondrial quality control mechanism that removes damaged mitochondria through mitophagy. The researchers link disruption of this pathway to glomerulonephritis, a form of kidney inflammation and dysfunction.
papers.why: Although this paper centers on kidney pathology rather than brain tissue, it offers mechanistic insight into PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy that is directly relevant to understanding mitophagy dysregulation in neurons.

papers.title: M6A-modified lncRNA RMRP facilitates mitophagy and promotes ox-LDL-induced endothelial cell injury by interacting with PTBP1 and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway.
papers.summary: This study examines how an RNA modification (m6A) affects a long non-coding RNA called RMRP in endothelial cells exposed to oxidized LDL, a key factor in atherosclerosis. The researchers found that modified RMRP promotes mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria) and worsens cell injury. Mechanistically, RMRP interacts with a protein called PTBP1 and turns on the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway to drive these effects.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on vascular endothelial cells rather than neurons, the molecular mechanisms linking m6A RNA modification, lncRNA regulation, and mitophagy could inform analogous studies of mitophagy regulation in neurons or glial cells within the brain.
